name: Earth
lede: Earth is the color of bare ground, a mid brown with an orange cast, and the name painters give to the oldest, cheapest and steadiest family of pigments: the ochres, siennas, umbers and green clays dug straight from the soil.

sections.title: A color named after the ground
sections.body:
Earth as a single swatch is a modern name. The color on this page, #A2653E, is the one Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary called Earth, a mid brown with an orange cast that ISCC-NBS files as brownish orange, and it turned up again among the names in the xkcd color survey of 2010 [36]. Who first used it as a color word is undocumented.

The plural is far older. Painters and dyers have long spoken of the earth colors, and Paterson defines them as the colors found in natural ground, which vary with what the soil contains [1]. Carbon or magnetite makes a black earth, iron silicate a green one, iron oxide a red, feldspar, kaolin and quartz a whitish earth, and limonite a yellow, with the oranges, ochres, russets, umbers and browns in between [1]. The earth pigments proper are the ochres, siennas and umbers that painters dig, wash and grind [1].

This article follows that family. The swatch is one point in it: its nearest named neighbors are [[orange-brown]] and [[sunburn]], [[sienna]] is 6.5 units away, and [[ochre]] 12.6 [36].

sections.title: What is in an earth
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium sorts the earth pigments by how much iron and manganese they hold [2]. Ochres are colored by iron oxides and hydroxides, and siennas are iron-rich earths with a few per cent of manganese oxide [2]. Umbers carry between 5 and 20 per cent manganese oxide beside 45 to 70 per cent iron oxide, and wads, with about half their weight in manganese, are dark brown to black [2]. The more manganese, the darker and cooler the brown.

Fire widens the range. The burnt earths, burnt umber, burnt ochre and burnt sienna, are the raw earths cooked to red heat [3]. That is why the paintbox pairs each of them, as [[raw-sienna]] and [[burnt-sienna|burnt sienna]] or [[raw-umber]] and [[burnt-umber]] [3][36].

Their names carry places, some of them doubtful. Siena gave its name to sienna, though Finlay suspects that sienna no longer comes from there [4][7]. [[umber]] is often traced to Umbria, but Ball, St Clair and Finlay all prefer the Latin for shadow, and Ball notes that European umber was mostly imported from Turkey [5][6][7]. Umber reached European painting around 1500, and in the 1620s Edward Norgate called burnt umber greasy and hard to work but of great use for shadows and hair [5].

Earths are also the steadiest colors a painter can buy. Paterson calls them the least prone to fade [1], and Rembrandt's restricted palette, leaning on earths, blacks and lakes, has aged well because he knew which materials would last [5].

sections.title: Green earth
sections.body:
Not every earth is warm. Green earth, sold as terre verte or Verona earth, is a clay colored by the minerals glauconite and celadonite [8]. It is weak in tint but permanent and stable in every medium [9]. Its use was worldwide: the Compendium lists it in first-century frescoes at Ajanta in India, in Byzantine and Orthodox icons, and in works by Michelangelo, Vermeer and Turner [8]. The copper pigment verditer may even owe its name to a corruption of *verde terra* [8].

Its great job was hidden. Cennini taught painters to lay flesh over an underlayer of green earth, and where the pink above has faded, the green now shows through, so that some medieval saints look ill [9][10]. Painters complained about it too. Pastoureau notes that earth greens covered poorly, and the Dutch painter van Hoogstraten found green earth too weak [11][5]. Still, Poussin and Vermeer kept Verona and Cyprus earth greens on their palettes [11]. The swatch our library calls [[green-earth]] is a pale yellow-green far from the pigment's grey-olive, 38.9 units from this page's color [36].

sections.title: Earths that were never rock
sections.body:
Some earths are not minerals at all. Humic earth forms from decayed plant matter and sits between lignite, a low-grade coal, and peat [13]. The best known is Cassel earth, called [[van-dyke-brown|Vandyke brown]] in England from about 1790, which came from deposits near Cologne and Cassel [5][13]. Ball notes that it is an earth only in the sense that it is dug from the ground [5].

Painters valued it as a transparent brown glaze. It has been reported in Rubens and Rembrandt and possibly Velázquez, and Gainsborough used it as Cologne earth [5]. It also darkened paintings on purpose: the Milanese restorer Giuseppe Molteni tinted his varnishes with Cassel earth to give old pictures a brown tone [14]. Today Gurney lists Van Dyke brown among the unreliable historic pigments [15].

sections.title: The oldest palette
sections.body:
The first palettes were earth palettes. Cave painters used iron-oxide reds and yellows, green earths, charcoal black, manganese brown and chalk or bone white [16]. Balfour-Paul suggests that people who had only earth colors must have found a fast blue dye a revelation [17].

Classical painting kept the earths at its core. The Alexander mosaic at Pompeii, a copy of a painting by Philoxenos, shows the restrained earth palette that Rome inherited from Greece [16]. Some earths were branded goods: Lemnian earth, from the island of Lemnos, was also sold as *terra sigillata*, sealed earth [18].

Cheapness defined them. Dürer paid nearly a hundred times more for ultramarine in 1521 than for some earths [19]. The painters' guild of Siena forbade members in 1355 to pass off red earth or red lead as fine vermilion [20].

sections.title: Shadows, grounds and a quarrel
sections.body:
Brown is a shade rather than a hue, and medieval artists, who prized pure precious materials, saw it as corrupt [21]. The Baroque reversed that judgment, and earth browns, from ochres and umber to Cassel earth, built the deep shadows of the seventeenth century [21]. Caravaggio's *Nativity with St. Francis and St. Lawrence* of 1609 is a very dark composition whose drama St Clair thinks probably owed much to umber [6], and after his bankruptcy Rembrandt relied on cheap earths, umber above all, for the shadows around his late faces [6]. Late in life Joshua Reynolds built his pictures on underpaintings of white, black, Indian red and raw umber [22].

The earths were also under the plaster. Fresco painters drew their designs in sinopia, a red-brown earth, and when a fire in 1944 stripped the frescoes from the Camposanto in Pisa, the drawings beneath came to light [21].

The Impressionists picked a quarrel with all this: Camille Pissarro boasted that he had removed the earth pigments from his palette, although they still turn up now and then, and the group mixed their browns from bright new synthetics instead [21]. In Monet's *Lavacourt under Snow* the olive, khaki and red-brown tones are mixed from bright pigments rather than earths [23]. Cézanne kept them, setting strong greens among subdued earths [23]. In 1888 Gauguin told Paul Sérusier to paint the ground the way he saw it, as red, with his best red, and the small result, *The Talisman*, launched the Nabis [23]. By 1920 the Purists Le Corbusier and Ozenfant had put ochres, reds and earths back in their stable major scale [24].

sections.title: What color is earth?
sections.body:
As one of the four elements, earth has no agreed color, and the sources disagree openly. Aristotle made earth black, and medieval physics followed him [25][26]. Alberti in the fifteenth century gave it ash grey [27]. The Upanishads called black the color of earth, Chinese five-element thought made earth yellow, and Leonardo paired yellow with earth as well [28][32]. Isidore of Seville read the white linen of the Temple curtain as earth [29], and a thirteenth-century French poem dressed a knight in brown stockings to signify the earth [30]. Tibetan prayer flags, hung in a fixed order, give earth the yellow flag [31].

The everyday word has its own branch. Khaki comes from a Hindustani word for dust or earth color, adopted by soldiers of the British Indian Army in the later nineteenth century [33]; our [[khaki]] swatch is greener than this one.

The planet complicated matters in the twentieth century. The phrase blue planet became common in the 1960s with the first spaceflights, and Paul Éluard had already called the earth blue like an orange in 1929 [35]. The same years made earth tones a fashion: after the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill, the first Earth Day in 1970 and the Blue Marble photograph of 1972, homes of the 1970s filled with [[avocado]], [[burnt-orange|burnt orange]] and [[harvest-gold|harvest gold]] [34].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Earth is one of the commonest colors in our archive, more common than 89 per cent of the named colors [37]. A color within six CIEDE2000 units of it covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,174 of 23,781 paintings, about one in twenty [37]. It is most common in the oldest work: the 1200s to 1400s carry it at 2.3 to 2.7 times the archive rate, while the 1600s fall below average [37]. The earliest and largest match is the [[art:aic-805|Funerary Papyrus of Tayuhenutmut]] of about 1069 BC, where it covers 73 per cent of the surface, which here means the papyrus itself [37].

It is strongest in Tibet, in 12 of 47 works, five times the archive rate, mostly thangkas and painted initiation cards; Pahari and Rajput painting carry it at about two and a half times [37]. Among European painters, Modigliani shows it in 5 of 18 works, among them [[art:nga-46520|Girl in a Green Blouse]] (1917), where it most likely reads as the sitter's warm skin; Tiepolo shows it in 8 of 40 [37]. The Impressionists bear out Pissarro's boast: only 3 of 140 Impressionist works here carry it, under half the archive rate [37]. It keeps family company, sharing canvases with sienna five times more often than chance and with burnt orange four and a half times [37].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test: an earth-colored patch may be paper, papyrus, gilding's red bole or a darkened varnish [37]. In Google Books, *earth* used as an adjective, the color sense, rises steeply after the 1940s, peaks in the 1960s and by 2010 stands at about half that level [38].

questions.q: What makes an umber darker and cooler than an ochre?
choices: It contains manganese oxide as well as iron oxide
It has been mixed with soot
It is a plant dye fixed onto clay
questions.answer: It contains manganese oxide as well as iron oxide

questions.q: Why do some medieval saints' faces look greenish today?
choices: The pink on top has faded and the green-earth underlayer shows through
Painters used green to show holiness
The panels were cleaned with acid
questions.answer: The pink on top has faded and the green-earth underlayer shows through
